cases.title: Data Dictionaries and LLMs: Context, Not Fine-Tuning
cases.problem: LLMs can read structured data, but column names rarely capture business meaning, relationships, valid values or operational rules. Without that context, models may misread fields, generate invalid queries or return confident but inaccurate conclusions.
cases.approach: Used a data dictionary to supply field definitions, formats, relationships, constraints and business rules. The post also separates this contextual adaptation from fine-tuning, which requires additional training and changes to the model's learned parameters.
cases.outcome: A shared layer between business knowledge, data structures and the LLM. The dictionary improves query accuracy, reduces hallucinated fields and keeps analysis within the dataset's real rules, vocabulary and boundaries.

cases.title: Bug & hotfix QA process: a branch map
cases.problem: A save-freeze bug on the live build of a gallery app needed a fast, disciplined path from report to fix without destabilising the next release.
cases.approach: Modelled the whole bug/hotfix flow as a git-style branch map: fork off master, run the triage lane (log and evidence, risk and dependency matrix, analytics-ranked priority), reproduce and fix, then merge back through QA retest, regression sweep and automation.
cases.outcome: A repeatable process where every ticket resolves into one of five documented outcomes: fixed, not reproducible, won't fix, duplicate or invalid. A clean fix feeds back as new test scenarios, so each build ships sturdier than the last.

cases.title: Data quality for history connections
cases.problem: Recife's historical records were scattered across inconsistent sources, duplicated names, conflicting dates, and messy formats that made any analysis unreliable.
cases.approach: Built a data-cleaning and storytelling pipeline: profiling the raw records, defining validation rules, de-duplicating entities, and documenting every transformation so the process stayed transparent and reproducible.
cases.outcome: A trustworthy, structured dataset that powers the Recife History Connections visualization, and a narrative that shows the cleaning decisions behind it.

cases.title: Self-maintenance of table test scripts with Claude
cases.problem: UI and table-based test scripts broke constantly as the product changed, and manual upkeep was eating into real testing time.
cases.approach: Used Claude to detect failing selectors and assertions, diagnose the cause, and propose self-healing updates to the scripts, keeping a human in the loop for review.
cases.outcome: Less time spent on brittle test maintenance and more confidence that the suite reflects the current product.

cases.title: Tracking Economic Impacts of a Carnival Bloco
cases.problem: A street carnival troça creates cultural, social and economic value, but its impact is rarely measured. Without data, its contribution to local businesses, workers and neighbourhoods remains largely anecdotal.
cases.approach: Used my own troça, Segura o Tonho, as a case study. Combined Recife City Hall data, Map of Frevo records, shirt sales, interviews and geolocation analysis with Python and pandas to map services, audiences, workers and the local economic chain.
cases.outcome: A proof of concept showing how carnival circulates wealth beyond the parade route. A troça of 300 people generated about R$9,500 in beverages and transport, benefited roughly 50 workers and connected suppliers and communities across a 10km radius.

cases.title: World Cup 2026: The Reality of the Numbers vs. Memory
cases.problem: After Brazil's 1–1 draw with Morocco, many fans felt the team had been completely overwhelmed. The post questions whether Morocco's intense opening pressure distorted how the entire match was remembered.
cases.approach: Reanalysed possession, shots, passes, positioning and the match timeline using SofaScore, FIFA and other football-data sources. AI supported data extraction, visualisation and cross-checking, followed by manual validation.
cases.outcome: Morocco clearly controlled the opening 20 minutes, reaching around 65% possession, but Brazil recovered before the half-hour mark and balanced much of the remaining game. The performance was not brilliant, but it was far more competitive than the post-match perception suggested.

cases.title: Traceability Matrix: risk-based test prioritization
cases.problem: One app with many parts that quietly share data, code, components and state, so a small change can break something several screens away. Testing everything is too slow, and testing the wrong things misses real defects.
cases.approach: Built a modules-and-features traceability matrix: inventory every subsystem, module and feature, record what each one shares with others, and count the most-shared hubs. Every pull request is traced back to the exact features its diff touched.
cases.outcome: Test effort follows risk instead of guesswork, the biggest blast-radius resources get tested first, and every feature stays accounted for. Less regression testing, caught earlier, with reasoning anyone can follow.
